title: Batteries
where: the Electrical shelf's Supply systems folder
folderRuns: Insulated systems and earth faults (built alongside this one), then Batteries
blurb: How a lead-acid cell works, capacity and discharge rate, charging stages, specific gravity, gassing and hydrogen, and cell faults.
from: any Brilliant chemistry or electricity course still reachable on brilliant.org that covers cells, and failing that Battery University (Cadex) as the public benchmark
others: Battery University, public battery manufacturers' handbooks and installation manuals for stationary lead-acid batteries (EnerSys, GNB/Exide, Yuasa, Hoppecke), BS EN IEC 62485-2 and IEEE 450 as titled public descriptions (single values only, no reproduced tables), OpenStax Chemistry 2e on electrochemistry, and HSE guidance on battery charging and hydrogen
syllabi: What a marine electrical engineer actually uses of this topic: the STCW Code Table A-III/6 (electro-technical officer) and A-III/1 competence lines that touch it, the MCA electro-technical officer and engineer officer syllabus lines (Electrotechnology), the public apprenticeship standards for an electrical or marine engineering technician on the Institute for Apprenticeships site, and the Pearson BTEC HN units that cover it. Exact lines. Also anything in Dan's electrical qualifications on batteries (likely little), so the course starts from first principles
later: Insulated systems and earth faults (same folder, built alongside: it owns insulated DC systems and earth detection)
scope: Large lead-acid batteries from first principles, in about this order (the brief may merge or split): (1) the cell: what happens at each plate as it discharges and charges (lead, lead dioxide, sulphuric acid, lead sulphate, water), told simply, and why a cell gives about 2 V; (2) state of charge: open-circuit voltage and specific gravity both track it, reading a hydrometer with temperature correction; (3) capacity and rate: ampere-hours, the C-rate, why capacity falls at high discharge rates (Peukert's law, using Exponentials and logarithms) and in the cold, and the voltage under load from internal resistance; (4) charging: constant current then constant voltage, the boost, equalise and float stages, and why voltage per cell is the controlled quantity (Electronics built the charger: use it, never re-teach it); (5) gassing and hydrogen: the gassing voltage, where hydrogen and oxygen come from, hydrogen's flammable range, and ventilation sized from the charging current as the standard's method does (Heat and fluids built gases and flow: use them); (6) strings of cells: series and parallel, cell imbalance, and why one weak cell limits the string; (7) ageing and faults: sulphation, stratification, grid corrosion, dry-out in valve-regulated cells, and how cell voltage, specific gravity, impedance and capacity tests find them (Statistics built trending: use it); (8) safety and other chemistries: short-circuit currents from a big battery, acid, isolation and working on DC, then nickel-cadmium and lithium-ion in outline and how they differ. Teach general large stationary and marine batteries; nothing on submarine battery design, layout or operation beyond CLAUDE.md's public outline (a large main battery exists). Examples from public, general marine and industrial equipment only; never how the Royal Navy or a particular boat does it, never submarine systems beyond CLAUDE.md's public outline, and never anything from Dan's SMQ books.
